abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: We update and extend the non-parametric test proposed in Ashley and Patterson (J Financ Quant Anal 21:221–227, 2014) – of the proposition that the (pre-whitened) daily stock returns for a firm are serially independent, and hence unpredictable from their own past. That paper applied this test to daily returns from 1962 to 1981 for several U.S. corporations and aggregate indices, finding mixed evidence against this null hypothesis of serial independence. The returns dataset is updated here to include thirteen firms which are currently more relevant, and the sample is extended through the end of 2023. We also update the simulation methodology here to properly account for the conditional heteroskedasticity in the daily returns data, so that the present results should now be more statistically reliable. The results are broadly in line with our earlier results, but they do suggest further avenues of research in this area.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In this paper we revisit the Ashley and Patterson (1) paper – denoted Ashley and Patterson (1) below – in which they used bootstrap simulation methods to nonparametrically test the ‘random walk’ null hypothesis that pre-whitened daily stock returns are otherwise serially iid, and hence not linearly forecastable from their own past.

Ashley and Patterson (1) were able to use something like 4,900 observations on the daily returns from 5 stocks – including Exxon Mobil, four fairly obscure firms (chosen at random), and also the daily returns from the CRSP equally-weighted and value-weighted stock indices. We chose 13 stocks for the analysis here. These were more-or-less randomly chosen from the group of stocks we thought that readers would find most interesting, plus Exxon Mobil (to overlap with the Ashley and Patterson (1) sample) and the two CRSP aggregate indices.1

As will be displayed below – in the illustrative example (using the 3M Company data) discussed in Sect. 2 – daily stock returns typically also exhibit marked conditional heteroskedasticity. Therefore, we improve here upon the ordinary bootstrap simulation methods used in Ashley and Patterson (1) – which were all that was available at the time – by instead using the wild bootstrap in all of the simulation work done here.2

In Sect. 2 we describe the Ashley and Patterson (1) test, as economically – in terms of journal-space – as possible; primarily referencing the original paper, and secondarily by utilizing the results we obtained for one of the stock return time series considered here (daily returns for the 3M Company) as an illustrative example. We then discuss the full set of results in Sect. 3.2, Table 2. Section 4, ends the paper with a summary, some conclusions as to how our current results compare to those of Ashley and Patterson (1), and a brief discussion as to some directions which our results suggest for future research.

sec.title: The Ashley and Patterson (1) test for serial independence in daily stock returns
sec.p: Ashley and Patterson (1) provides a nice review of the literature leading up to the AP test – e.g., citing the classic Fama (4) article in this area. The Ashley and Patterson (1) article itself is readily available at https://www.jstor.org/stable/2330739, so there is no need to repeat their review here. We will, however, comment later in the paper (in passing) on some of the subsequent literature – in particular, just a bit on Corrado and Schatzberg (3) and on Mills (7).

On the other hand, we still find the AP test of intense interest. Now, however, our interest in the AP test centers more on using the test’s rejection P-value as an observable measure of the degree to which one can discern in the data evidence for a ‘restoring force’ in the market dynamics, representing – likely nonlinear – dynamics which are missing in the specification of the random walk model of Eq. (1).

What made AP’s concern of scientific value is that they proposed an observationally falsifiable hypothesis based on it: the random walk hypothesis implies that an empirically observable sequence of T daily stock returns should, they conjectured, ‘wander off’ from the trend line at least as far – and as often – as one would ‘statistically expect’ based on this hypothesis. But, crucially, it should not, on average, wander off less than this.

Thus, if this null hypothesis (positing that the geometric random walk model adequately describes the generating mechanism for daily stock returns) is false – say, because some nonlinear mechanism kicks in to ‘pull’ returns back toward the trend line whenever they deviate too far away from it – then one ought to find that the observed sequence of daily stock returns ‘wanders off’ from the trend line less far (or less frequently) than one might ‘statistically expect’ it to, based on the random walk null hypothesis. Thus, the possibility of a usable scientific (one-sided) hypothesis test arises.

As noted in Sect. 1 above, the present work will improve on Ashley and Patterson (1) in several respects. In particular, we are now be able to utilize much longer samples on stock returns for U.S. firms than were available in 1986. And we will also here use data on a sample of firms which is both more numerous and more likely of current interest. In addition, we will also modernize the simulation technique used in constructing the test, to allow for the conditional heteroskedasticity in the daily stock return data; this was not possible at the time Ashley and Patterson (1) was written.

The remainder of this section explicitly considers the application of the Ashley and Patterson (1) test to the daily returns (exclusive of dividends) for the stock in one of the companies selected for analysis here: the 3M Company. This firm was selected from the group entirely because it was listed at the top of Table 1.

A time plot of the 3M Company daily returns observations over this 1962 - 2023 sample period is displayed as Fig. 1 below; Fig. 2 displays a histogram of these data, with a corresponding Gaussian density plot superimposed for comparison. These plots show that – as is typical of daily returns data – the 3M Company returns at first glance appear to be normally distributed and covariance stationary. On closer inspection of the histogram, however, one can also clearly see that these returns are leptokurtic: more sharply peaked and thicker-tailed than would be data drawn from a Gaussian distribution, although they do appear to be symmetrically distributed. And, on closer inspection of the time plot (Fig. 1), one can clearly see the time-dependent bursts of higher variance typical of a time series exhibiting strong evidence of conditional heteroskedasticity. Thus, the 3M Company returns at first glance appear to be Gaussian and covariance stationary, but are actually neither, as is the case with all of the other returns data we consider here.4Fig. 1

sec.title: The stock returns data used here and our AP test results
The sample data
sec.p: Table 1 concisely describes our present, substantially more extensive, data set, obtained – as was the sample data set in AP (1986) – from the CRSP website.11

We pursued no formal strategy in selecting the 15 daily return series listed in Table 1, but the following considerations were applied:
We felt that it was essential to again include both the value-weighted and the equally-weighted CRSP indices (VWRETX and EWRETX) in the analysis.
It also seemed essential to include Exxon Mobil (XOM) in the analysis, because this was the only one – among the stocks in the Ashley and Patterson (1) group of firms – which survived for very long after the end of the sample period for that study.
Beyond that, we wanted our current sample of firms to both exhibit a reasonable variety of firm sizes – as quantified by their market capitalizations – and to also exemplify a variety of different industries.
The reader might conceivably take the phrase ‘a variety of industries’ above to indicate that perhaps we were vitally interested in obtaining a group of 13 individual stock return time series whose sample cross-correlations were so small that we could argue – as we did, to some extent, in Ashley and Patterson (1) – that one could use the standard Fisher (5) result to combine them in a portmanteau test. That was not the case, however: We merely sought variety in our sample of firms, so that our results would be of greater interest to ourselves and to our prospective readers.12
The message we hope that the reader takes from Table 1 is that this sample of firms – while in no objective sense ‘representative’ – is nevertheless quite a variegated and, we think, an interesting one.
We note that the mean return for each stock is tiny because these are daily returns; and that – more importantly – these figures vary quite a bit across the firms, as do the reported market capitalization and variance estimates for the firms. These market capitalization estimates are reported without specific dates; they are included here for rough comparison purposes only.

sec.title: Our AP test results
A brief summary of our conclusions from these results – and some ideas as to research questions of future interest
sec.p: First, perhaps the most conspicuous conclusion we draw from this revisiting of the original Ashley and Patterson (1) paper, nonparametrically testing the ‘random walk’ null hypothesis that pre-whitened daily stock returns are otherwise serially iid – is that the 1986 work has held up remarkably well. And this is despite the fact that our ‘re-do’ uses something like three times as much sample data on 13 (instead of 5) firms – and this is notwithstanding the fact that our present work updates the bootstrap simulation methodology used to now account for the considerable conditional heteroskedasticity in all of these daily stock return time series.

Indeed, our qualitative results here are pretty much the same as those obtained in Ashley and Patterson (1): There is notable evidence against the null hypothesis that daily returns are serially iid for the returns in some firms, but definitely not for others. Overall, the evidence against this null hypothesis at first glance looks rather weak. But, if one assumes that the returns data are independently distributed, and applies the Fisher Combined Probability Test, then the null hypothesis is rejected with a P-value of 0.024, which is not all that much larger than the 0.014 value obtained on the Fisher test in Ashley and Patterson (1)

From this point of view, we see the P-value column of Table 2 as likely indicating that the firms fall into three groups: a group whose stock trades in markets with relatively strong restoring forces (3M Company, Exxon Mobile, IBM, Nike, Pepsi Cola, and Tesla), a group whose stock trades in markets where we cannot detect such restoring forces (Pfizer and Tyson Foods), and a remaining group of stocks trading in markets constituting intermediate cases.

This observation suggests that it might be worthwhile to compute AP test P-value results for daily returns on a substantially larger sample of firms.18 One could then attempt to quantify and model the reasons why these restoring forces arise. Perhaps efforts along these lines would even begin to shed more light than is currently available on the origin and dynamics of the conditional heteroskedasticity long known to be characteristic of daily corporate stock returns.

In particular, we use the Gonçalves and Kilian (6) formulation of the wild bootstrap here, because it is optimized for the presence of both conditional heteroskedasticity and serial correlation. The wild bootstrap is quite simple and intuitive, but it is fairly well known – and well-described in Gonçalves and Kilian (6)—so space limitations preclude describing it at any length here. In essence, the wild bootstrap substitutes an assumption that the pre-whitened returns are symmetrically and independently distributed for the usual bootstrap assumption that they are identically and independently distributed. This symmetry assumption is quite reasonable for the present data set. See Sect. 2 for a bit more on this topic.

It is easy to eliminate this observation from the sample, which yields a time plot (and histogram) which both look a bit ‘nicer.’ The estimated pre-whitening model is little affected by this elimination. More importantly, the plot of the cumulative sum of the pre-whitened returns – discussed below – is almost completely unaffected by this elimination, so that the AP test result rejection P-value reported in Table 2 for this stock changes only from 0.059 to to 0.060. The AP test is evidently very robust to outliers.

We will return to this topic in Sect. 3.2 below, where results related to this independence assumption are discussed.

Recall, that the daily returns for each stock are being modeled in this way so as to eliminate any observed tendency for the time series to ‘wander back’ toward the trend line to a larger degree than is implied by the null hypothesis of serial independence – i.e., the random walk model of Eq. 1 – due merely to un-modeled serial correlation.
